title: EPA Proposes Repeal of the Clean Power Plan
description_short: EPA announced a proposed repeal of the Clean Power Plan, reversing the Obama-era climate rule for power plants.
description_medium: On October 10, 2017, EPA proposed repealing the Clean Power Plan, the Obama administration’s rule for reducing carbon emissions from existing power plants. Administrator Scott Pruitt announced the change as the first step toward replacing the plan. The proposal began a rulemaking process; it did not itself erase the standards then in force.
description_long: The Environmental Protection Agency announced its proposal to repeal the Clean Power Plan on October 10, 2017. The plan, adopted under President Barack Obama, set a federal framework for reducing carbon pollution from existing power plants. EPA Administrator Scott Pruitt presented repeal as a shift away from the previous administration’s approach to climate regulation. Because this was a proposed rule, states, utilities, and the public could respond during the rulemaking before EPA finalized a replacement. The proposal did not immediately change the obligations that applied to power plants. It opened a broader dispute over how much authority the federal government should use to curb emissions from electricity generation and how that work should be divided between federal and state regulators. The administration later issued the Affordable Clean Energy rule as its replacement, but that later action was separate from the October announcement. The proposal marked the start of a major reversal in federal climate policy, while its practical effects depended on subsequent rules and court decisions.

description_long: Donald Trump granted a posthumous pardon to boxer John Arthur “Jack” Johnson on May 24, 2018. The prosecution took place amid racist hostility toward Johnson and his success in a sport dominated by white champions. He served time in prison and spent years abroad before returning to the United States. Johnson died in 1946. The pardon followed a long campaign by activists, lawmakers, and sports figures who argued that the conviction was racially motivated and unjust. Trump’s clemency order removed the federal conviction’s legal stigma, though it could not undo the harm Johnson suffered during his life. The action was included among the president’s clemency grants and drew renewed attention to how criminal law had been used against interracial relationships. title: Iran Nuclear Talks Collapse After Five Rounds
description_short: Iran Nuclear Talks Collapse After Five Rounds
description_medium: Five rounds of U.S.-Iran nuclear talks took place in April and May 2025, mediated by Oman. Negotiators disagreed over whether Iran could continue uranium enrichment: U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff first floated limited enrichment, then demanded its dismantlement, while Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called enrichment non-negotiable. The talks stalled before U.S. strikes began; the available account does not detail the final negotiating positions.
description_long: From April through May 2025, the Trump administration conducted five rounds of nuclear negotiations with Iran — the first such direct US-Iran diplomatic contact since 2017 — mediated by Oman and held in Muscat and Rome. US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff initially floated allowing Iran to enrich uranium at 3.67%, then reversed course demanding total dismantlement of all enrichment capability, which he called a red line. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called enrichment non-negotiable. By the fifth round in Rome on May 23, Oman's mediator reported some but not conclusive progress. Witkoff left early. Iran had accelerated enrichment to 60% purity, enough to produce material for over a dozen weapons within weeks. A bipartisan letter signed by 52 senators and 177 representatives warned Trump against any deal allowing Iran to retain any enrichment capability. Talks formally collapsed when Trump, frustrated with the pace, privately issued ultimatums to Tehran and then ordered military strikes without returning to negotiations, bypassing Congress entirely.

title: Trump DOJ Argues Employers Can Fire LGBTQ+ Workers
description_short: Trump DOJ Argues Employers Can Fire LGBTQ+ Workers
description_medium: In 2019, the Trump Justice Department argued in federal court that Title VII did not prohibit employment discrimination against LGBTQ+ workers. The Supreme Court rejected that position in Bostock v. Clayton County in 2020, ruling that firing employees for being gay or transgender violates the statute’s ban on discrimination because of sex.
description_long:
The Trump Justice Department filed briefs in 2019 arguing that Title VII of the Civil Rights Act did not protect LGBTQ+ employees from workplace discrimination. That position differed from the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission’s interpretation and asked courts to permit employers to fire workers for being gay or transgender. Civil-rights organizations criticized the argument as a threat to workplace protections.

The Supreme Court resolved the legal question in Bostock v. Clayton County in 2020. In a 6–3 decision, it held that Title VII’s ban on discrimination “because of sex” covers firing employees for being gay or transgender, rejecting the administration’s interpretation. The Court’s decision applied the statute; it did not amend the text of Title VII. The Justice Department argued that the statute referred to biological sex; the Court’s ruling established protections for LGBTQ+ workers nationwide. The decision remains controlling precedent.
